extracted.intended_audience: researchers (authors & reviewers), journal editors, publishers, funders, institutions, and others interested in giving or using public preprint feedback
extracted.subtask_description: Practical FAQ and normative guidance for providing, locating, using, and responding to public feedback on preprints; includes principles for constructive reviews, posting venue considerations, equity recommendations, and advice for authors, editors, and funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAST — Focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Focused: on the science, not the individuals or journal to which the paper might be submitted. Respect the existing focus and scope of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving feedback, keep comments targeted to the manuscript’s scientific claims, methods, and scope rather than attacking authors or their choice of venue. Avoid suggesting changes that fall outside the stated focus of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAST — Appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate: use a polite, respectful, and constructive tone. Reflect on your motivations and biases. Behave with integrity, following ethical conduct expected in all research activities. Call out inappropriate behaviors or critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain civility and professionalism; consider whether tone or framing could be harmful. If you see genuinely inappropriate reviews or behaviour, explicitly call them out. Reflect on competing interests before posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAST — Specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific: consider whether claims are supported by the data and provide clear, actionable, and useful suggestions for the authors to improve the work. Distinguish between critical vs optional modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague statements. Point to exact figures, analyses, or text and offer concrete ways to verify, fix, or improve claims. Separate essential critiques (that threaten conclusions) from optional enhancements.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAST — Transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent: post feedback publicly, sharing information on the limits of your expertise and competing interests. Acknowledge errors & credit colleagues who contributed to the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose any relevant conflicts of interest and the scope of your expertise when commenting. If you change your opinion or make an error, update the public record and credit collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for author response
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever you find preprint reviews, be sure to check for an author response to make sure you are considering their perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before treating feedback as definitive, search for replies from authors (on the same thread, elsewhere on the web, or by searching the review URL) so you understand whether concerns were addressed or clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to post — Visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Visibility: Using a preprint server’s commenting section is often the easiest way to ensure that your review is likely to be seen by those who view the preprint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer platforms that are directly linked from the preprint record when you want authors and readers to see your feedback. If the server doesn’t display external discussion (e.g., tweets), consider posting where the preprint record will point to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to post — Permanence and citability
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanence and citability: If your review has a persistent identifier (PID) such as a DOI and relevant metadata, it will be easier for others to cite your work, include it in ORCID, and for services to index it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose venues that mint DOIs or otherwise promise long-term preservation if you want your review to be citable and discoverable; otherwise, document reviews in a manner that enables citation and indexing where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to post — Limitations on participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations on participation: While many venues allow anyone to post, some reviewing projects aren’t open to all: they may function as journal clubs or use editors to identify reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check platform policies about who may contribute and whether moderation or editorial selection applies; this affects both whether you can post and how your review will be treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to find preprint feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Many preprint servers have commenting functionality, and some link to social media commentary or external peer review sites. Use server dashboards, Twitter searches (search the preprint URL), Sciety, Early Evidence Base, and EuropePMC links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preprint server dashboards (e.g., bioRxiv evaluation dashboard), targeted Twitter searches with the preprint URL, and aggregator services like Sciety or Early Evidence Base. If reviews are on platforms without author-response features (e.g., GitHub), search for the review URL to find related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity in finding and amplifying reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek to reduce availability bias and Matthew effects by looking beyond your network: search regional servers, publish/search in multiple languages, and find preprints that have not yet been amplified on blogs or Twitter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively include regional preprint servers (e.g., AfricArxiv, RINarxiv), conduct multilingual keyword searches, and avoid relying solely on Twitter as your source. Encourage review coordinators to adopt inclusive policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive feedback — general conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the same principles that guide constructive private review apply to public review: be constructive, focus on improvement, and include actionable suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat public feedback as you would a professional review: explain reasoning, provide evidence, suggest experiments/analyses or clarifications, and separate major concerns from minor suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone, bias, and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on your motivations and biases, behave with integrity, and avoid ad hominem attacks. Scientists need critical but fair feedback; rubber stamping harms reviewer reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of both over-critical and over-collegial tendencies (e.g., 'pulling punches'). Declare competing interests and be willing to be challenged by others who can validate or dispute your critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling misleading, inappropriate, or harmful reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: If you see a review that is disrespectful, ad hominem, or merely mistaken, reply to the review to point this out. If associated with the authors, prudently declare competing interests when refuting comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First attempt a courteous, rational public reply to correct the record. If that escalates or is harmful, flag to moderators or use platform reporting tools (e.g., Twitter/Disqus flagging). Always disclose relationships to the authors when refuting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to feedback as an author
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, it’s good practice to respond to all feedback. However, distinguish well-founded criticism from trolling or repetitive/ill-informed comments; respond publicly when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond courteously and address points with evidence or clarification. For persistent or harmful trolling, consider moderation/flagging or limited engagement. Use author responses to add context and rebut criticisms that might otherwise influence editors or evaluators.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to request public feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: By explicitly requesting public feedback on your preprint, and specifying the time frame and type of feedback you need, you help readers provide more useful input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announce a deadline and target areas (e.g., 'My co-authors and I welcome public feedback on our preprint, ideally by [DATE]. We are especially interested in [statistics, etc].'). Post the request on the preprint record or via social media to invite reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaining credit or recognition for public preprint review
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal systems are limited, but you can use services and profiles to get recognition: join the ASAPbio Preprint Reviewer Recruitment Network; add reviews to your CV or ORCID profile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Recruitment Network to volunteer your reviews as work samples. Add your review as an item on ORCID (select 'Other') or list it under a peer-review/comments section on your CV. Prefer venues that mint DOIs for reviews to aid indexing and citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors should read preprint feedback critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprint reviews should be read critically with the knowledge that many venues are unmoderated and/or do not require the disclosure of competing interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should verify the provenance of reviews, look for author responses, and weigh anonymous or unmoderated comments appropriately when using preprint feedback in editorial decisions or triage.

rubrics_metrics.name: How journals and publishers can encourage public feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can encourage public preprint feedback by asking editors to look for it, posting reviews on preprints, participating in reviewer recruitment networks, and announcing such policies to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt policies that use preprint feedback in editorial workflows, publicly post reviews to preprints (eLife example), and participate in initiatives (e.g., Preprint Reviewer Recruitment Network) that surface reviewer activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: How funders and institutions can encourage public preprint feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders and institutions can endorse inclusion of refereed preprints as peer-reviewed articles in applications, enable listing of preprint reviews as scholarly outputs, and educate evaluators about assessing these outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow applicants to cite refereed preprints and attached reviews in grant/hiring materials; support metadata or tagging that identifies outputs as reviews; train reviewers/evaluators to consider preprint reviews appropriately.
